topic: Geographic Themes (Three from the SL list)
subject: geography

items.title: The Ring of Fire is a 40,000 km horseshoe of subduction zones
items.claim: What is the Pacific Ring of Fire?

options.text: A single underwater volcano in Hawaii
A roughly horseshoe-shaped zone around the Pacific basin where multiple plate boundaries — mostly subduction — produce around 90% of the world's earthquakes and around 75% of active volcanoes
A pattern visible only from satellites

items.reveal:
The Ring follows the boundaries of the Pacific Plate against the Eurasian, North American, Philippine, Cocos, Nazca and Australian plates. Major subduction zones include the Aleutian Trench, Japan Trench, Mariana Trench, Tonga Trench, Peru-Chile Trench.

Notable Ring events: 1960 Valdivia (Chile, M9.5, largest ever recorded); 1964 Great Alaska (M9.2); 2004 Sumatra-Andaman (M9.1); 2011 Tohoku (M9.0). Volcanoes include Mount St Helens (1980), Pinatubo (1991), Krakatoa (1883) and Tambora (1815).

The USGS tracks around 50 earthquakes per day globally; most are Ring-of-Fire events too small to feel.
items.why: Hazard distribution follows tectonic structure. Building codes in Tokyo, Anchorage, Santiago and Wellington are calibrated to subduction-zone physics — and the underlying geology dictates the risk profile of entire economies.

items.title: The boreal forest is the world's largest terrestrial biome
items.claim: Which is the world's largest forest biome?

options.text: The boreal forest (taiga) — a circumpolar belt across Russia, Canada, Alaska and Scandinavia totalling around 1.5 billion hectares; larger than all tropical rainforests combined and storing more carbon

items.reveal:
Boreal forest covers around 30% of all forest area and stores an estimated 30-40% of terrestrial carbon — much of it in deep peat and permafrost soils. Russia's taiga alone is around 12 million km².

Dominant species: spruce, fir, pine, larch, birch. Wildlife: brown bear, lynx, wolverine, capercaillie, moose. Productivity per hectare is lower than the Amazon, but the area is far larger.

Climate change is intensifying boreal wildfires — Siberia 2019-21, Canada 2023 — releasing carbon and potentially turning some boreal regions into net carbon sources. Permafrost thaw could release vast methane and CO₂.
items.why: The Amazon dominates public attention as 'the lungs of the planet'. The boreal forest is larger, stores more carbon, and is increasingly fire-prone — but receives a fraction of the press coverage.

items.title: Scotland is still rising — England is sinking
items.claim: What is happening to the British Isles vertically due to glacial isostatic adjustment?

options.text: Both are stable — Britain has fully recovered from the last Ice Age
Scotland and northern England rise by 1-2 mm/year as crust rebounds from glacial loading; southern and eastern England sink by around 1 mm/year
All of Britain is sinking equally
The British Isles tilt is not measurable

items.reveal:
When the last ice sheet melted (about 10,000 years ago), the depressed crust began to rise. The mantle's slow viscous flow means rebound is still happening. GPS networks (BIGF, the British Isles GNSS Facilities) measure the motion directly.

Net result for relative sea level: southern England experiences faster sea-level rise than would be expected from climate alone, while northern Scotland experiences slower (or even falling) relative sea level. This is one reason why Thames and Hull tidal defences face accelerating pressure.

Fenno-Scandinavia is rising even faster (10 mm/year in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia).
items.why: Climate-change sea-level projections must be combined with local geophysics. A coast is rising or sinking on its own terms, and the climate signal sits on top of that.
